title: Polymorphism
intro: **Polymorphism** means different types can be used through the same interface. If several classes each have a `speak()` method, a loop can call `speak()` on any of them without checking which class it is. Python cares about what an object can **do**, not what it **is** — this is called **duck typing**.

questions.prompt: Built-ins work the same way: `len()` works on anything that defines `__len__`.
questions.explanation: Neither class inherits from the other — they just share a method name.

questions.prompt: Write classes `Duck` and `Robot`, each with a `speak()` method returning `"Quack"` and `"Beep"`. Then store `[x.speak() for x in things]` in `sounds`, where `things` is `[Duck(), Robot(), Duck()]`.

tests.name: classes
tests.code: assert Duck().speak() == 'Quack' and Robot().speak() == 'Beep', 'Each class should speak its own sound.'

questions.explanation: The list comprehension never asks what type each thing is.
One function, three types — built-in polymorphism.

questions.prompt: Write `total_area(shapes)` that returns the sum of `shape.area()` for any objects that have an `area()` method, rounded to 2 decimals.
questions.solution:
def total_area(shapes):
    return round(sum(s.area() for s in shapes), 2)

tests.name: given
tests.code: assert total_area([Circle(1), Square(3)]) == 12.14, 'total_area should add up the areas.'

tests.name: duck

questions.explanation: Duck typing: a new shape class works without changing `total_area`.

options.text: Use different types through the same method names

questions.explanation: Code that calls `area()` works with every shape that provides it.

questions.prompt: The loop crashes with *AttributeError* on the third shape. Fix the class so it fits the same interface as the others.
questions.hint: All shapes must use the same method name.
questions.explanation: Polymorphism only works when everyone shares the interface.

questions.prompt: Fill in the special method name so `len(playlist)` works.
questions.hint: `len()` calls a method with double underscores.
questions.explanation: Defining `__len__` lets your object work with `len()`.

questions.prompt: Write payment classes `Card`, `PayPal` and `Voucher`, each with `pay(amount)` returning `"Paid 12.50 by card"`, `"… by PayPal"`, `"… by voucher"` (2 decimals). Then write `checkout(method, amount)` that calls `method.pay(amount)` and returns its result.

tests.name: each
tests.code: assert [checkout(m, 12.5) for m in (Card(), PayPal(), Voucher())] == ['Paid 12.50 by card', 'Paid 12.50 by PayPal', 'Paid 12.50 by voucher'], 'Each payment method should describe itself.'

tests.name: new method

questions.hint: `checkout` just calls `pay` — no `if` on the type.
questions.explanation: Adding a payment method later means writing a class, not editing `checkout`.

questions.hint: `str()` asks each object how to show itself.
questions.explanation: Every type knows how to turn itself into text.

questions.prompt: Write `CsvExporter` and `JsonExporter`, each with a `name` attribute (`"csv"`, `"json"`) and `export(rows)` for a list of dictionaries. CSV: header line, then values joined by commas, lines joined by `\n`. JSON: `json.dumps(rows)`. Then `export_all(rows, exporters)` returns a dictionary name → exported text.

tests.name: value
tests.code:
rows = [{'id': 1, 'city': 'Lima'}, {'id': 2, 'city': 'Oslo'}]
out = export_all(rows, [CsvExporter(), JsonExporter()])
assert out == {'csv': 'id,city\n1,Lima\n2,Oslo', 'json': '[{"id": 1, "city": "Lima"}, {"id": 2, "city": "Oslo"}]'}, 'Check both export formats.'

questions.hint: Each exporter has the same two parts: `name` and `export`.
questions.explanation: A common interface lets new formats plug in without changing `export_all`.
